20261124-fe45819a-a1.topic: What Daily Life Was Like for Artisans in Ancient Egypt
20261124-fe45819a-a1.description:
Nestled in the arid hills of western Thebes over three thousand years ago lay Set Ma’at, meaning The Place of Truth. Known today as Deir el-Medina, this secluded desert village was home to the royal stonecutters, sculptors, draughtsmen, and scribes who carved and painted the magnificent tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

Away from the grand monuments of the pharaohs, these specialized artisans led remarkably structured daily lives. From eight-day work shifts inside subterranean tombs to domestic squabbles, legal rights for women, and history's first recorded labor strike over delayed grain rations, explore what life was truly like for the ordinary people behind ancient Egypt's eternal wonders.

20261124-59f8716e-a1.topic: A Day in the Life of a Glassmaker in 15th-Century Venice
20261124-59f8716e-a1.title: Why You Wouldn't Survive a Day as a Venetian Glassmaker
20261124-59f8716e-a1.description:
In 1470, the small island of Murano in the Venetian lagoon held a global monopoly on the finest glass in the Western world, including the clear invention known as cristallo. Behind this incredible luxury was a brutal reality for ordinary artisans. Trapped on the island by the Venetian Republic under penalty of death or imprisonment, glassmakers worked near roaring furnaces reaching eleven hundred degrees Celsius.

Step into the shoes of Alvise, an assistant glassmaker navigating pre-dawn shifts, blistering radiant heat, and heavy trade secrets. From drinking diluted table wine to survive dehydration to crushing imported Syrian plant ash, discover the quiet, relentless daily labor that built Venice's legendary glass empire.

Chapters:
0:00 The Midnight Call of the Furnace
